concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP
concepts.reason: NOOP exposes checkpoint status without transferring frames.

claims.text: A checkpoint moves transactions from the WAL back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) schedules a checkpoint after a transaction commits when the WAL contains at least N frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint are PASSIVE.
claims.quote: The wal_autocheckpoint pragma can be used to invoke this interface from SQL. Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE .

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop before processing a WAL page past any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before its content moves into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: Read performance deteriorates as the WAL grows because checking it for content takes time proportional to its size.
claims.quote: read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional to the size

claims.text: Crossing a reader's end mark could overwrite database content that the reader is actively using.
claims.quote: The checkpoint has to stop at that point because otherwise it might overwrite part of the database file that the reader is actively using.

claims.text: A checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that position on its next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits using the busy-handler until no writer exists and all readers use the most recent database snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL blocks new database writers while it is pending.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART additionally waits until all readers read only from the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the WAL from its beginning.
claims.quote: until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE adds truncation of the WAL to zero bytes immediately before a successful return to RESTART behavior.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP checkpoints zero frames and serves to retrieve pnLog and pnCkpt status.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: A checkpoint returns SQLITE_BUSY if another process's checkpoint prevents acquisition of the exclusive checkpoint lock.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: By default, the thread performing the COMMIT that crosses the WAL size limit also runs the automatic checkpoint.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: As of SQLite 3.11.0, released 2016-02-15, a single transaction's WAL should be proportional in size to that transaction.
claims.quote: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself.

claims.text: If the busy-handler returns zero before writer-lock acquisition or while waiting for readers, the checkpoint proceeds using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: When the writer lock is unavailable, a configured busy-handler controls retries until it returns zero or the lock is acquired.
claims.quote: If the writer lock cannot be obtained immediately, and a busy-handler is configured, it is invoked and the writer lock retried until either the busy-handler returns 0 or the lock is successfully obtained.

claims.text: Failure to acquire the checkpoint lock because another checkpoint is running does not invoke the busy-handler.
claims.quote: Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: pnCkpt includes frames checkpointed before the current sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 call.
claims.quote: If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: Passing N less than or equal to zero to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint replaces any callback previously registered using sqlite3_wal_hook.
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .

claims.text: Registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook disables automatic checkpointing configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: Continuously overlapping readers can prevent checkpoint completion indefinitely and allow unbounded WAL growth.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Checkpoint starvation can be avoided by attempting checkpoints during reader gaps when no process reads the database.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: The WAL cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL permits new database readers to continue unimpeded while it is pending.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: A writer rewinds the WAL when its entire content has been transferred and synced and no reader uses the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: A checkpoint normally does not truncate the WAL file, with journal_size_limit identified as an exception.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set).

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: Writers omit WAL sync at transaction commit when PRAGMA synchronous is NORMAL.
claims.quote: (Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)

claims.text: When zDb is NULL or empty and the operation targets all attached WAL databases, pnLog and pnCkpt outputs are undefined.
claims.quote: then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: During an all-attached-databases operation, SQLITE_BUSY does not prevent attempts on remaining WAL databases and is returned at the end.
claims.quote: If an SQLITE_BUSY error is encountered when processing one or more of the attached WAL databases, the operation is still attempted on any remaining attached databases and SQLITE_BUSY is returned at the end.

claims.text: Targeting an attached database that is not in WAL mode returns SQLITE_OK with pnLog and pnCkpt both set to -1.
claims.quote: If database zDb is the name of an attached database that is not in WAL mode, SQLITE_OK is returned and both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.

limitations: Only the three supplied source excerpts were used; no tools, external lookup, writes, or agents were used.
The three-deepening-pass cap was reached. Pass 3 added 22.2222% new information; two consecutive passes below 5% did not occur.

The 36-claim output cap limits coverage. At least one further pass could cover explicit API error paths, PASSIVE sync conditions, and successful TRUNCATE output values; the packet cannot establish how many additional passes would remain productive.
All six deepening questions were considered against the accumulated claims. Mechanism, boundaries, exceptions, and primary-source wording supplied most additions; historical evidence supplied f18.
The packet documents SQLite 3.11.0 transaction-size behavior but does not establish the history of checkpoint mode introduction or changes in expert understanding.

The packet supplies no independent expert disagreement. S1 broadly warns that RESTART and TRUNCATE might block readers, whereas S2 says RESTART does not impede readers; their conditions are insufficient to reconcile these statements.

S1's application-initiated checkpoint overview lists three subtypes and later refers to RESET; S2 explicitly documents PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE, and NOOP. The packet does not establish the origin or chronology of this wording difference.
No live concept inventory or unavailable runtime references were assumed.
